people.name: Supenn Harrison
body: In the summer of 1976, fairgoers at the Minnesota State Fair lined up at a small booth selling Supenn Harrison's egg rolls. Her coworkers loved them, and that encouraged her to try a State Fair stand. The booth went on to run for 25 years, and it was the start of a business that brought Thai food to Minnesota.

Harrison grew up in Thailand and came to the University of Minnesota as a graduate student in the 1970s. Her family's restaurant history puts her arrival in 1972. When she finished graduate school she could not find work in her field, so she took a janitorial job at Abbott Northwestern Hospital.

In 1979 Harrison bought the Gopher Grill on Lake Street in Minneapolis, swapped the fryers for woks, and renamed it the Siam Cafe. Her company calls it the first Thai restaurant in Minnesota, and Mpls.St.Paul Magazine calls it Minneapolis's first official Thai restaurant. In 1983 she opened the first Sawatdee restaurant in St. Paul's Lowertown, and the Minneapolis Star and Tribune gave it four stars. A Minneapolis flagship followed in 1986. Later restaurants opened in Bloomington (1990), St. Cloud (1994, run by her sister Noi), and Maple Grove (2002). In 2010 her daughters Cyndy and Jenny took over day-to-day operations.

Harrison's work reached past her restaurants. According to the Asia Matters for America project, a generous donation from Harrison in late 2003 made it possible to found Wat Thai of Minnesota, the Buddhist temple now in St. Louis Park. She was also featured in Asian Flavors, a Twin Cities PBS and Minnesota Historical Society Press documentary about how Asian immigrants shaped Minnesota's food and economy.
keyFacts: 1972: Came from Thailand to the University of Minnesota for graduate school, by her company's account.
1976: Opened a Minnesota State Fair egg-roll booth, which ran for 25 years.
1979: Turned the Gopher Grill on Lake Street into the Siam Cafe, described by her company as Minnesota's first Thai restaurant.
1983: Opened the first Sawatdee in St. Paul's Lowertown. 1986: Opened the Minneapolis flagship.
2003: Her donation enabled the founding of Wat Thai of Minnesota, according to Asia Matters for America.
2010: Her daughters took over daily operations.
people.connectToWork: A person's name, language or birthplace in Thailand may lead a form or a colleague to group them with Hmong, Lao or Karen Minnesotans, some of whom were born in refugee camps in Thailand. What would you ask, rather than assume, about how someone came to Minnesota before you choose a service or an interpreter?

people.name: Tammy Duckworth
body: On November 12, 2004, Army helicopter pilot Tammy Duckworth was flying a Black Hawk over Iraq for the Illinois Army National Guard when a rocket-propelled grenade hit the aircraft. She lost both legs, and her right arm was saved only after a 13-hour emergency surgery. She then spent about a year recovering at Walter Reed Army Medical Center, where she began advocating for fellow wounded soldiers.

Duckworth was born in Bangkok on March 12, 1968, the daughter of Lamai, a Thai mother of Chinese descent, and Franklin Duckworth, an American father and veteran who worked in development aid. The family lived in Thailand and Singapore before moving to Hawaii when she was 16, and for a time they relied on public assistance. She is fluent in Thai and Indonesian. She graduated from the University of Hawaii in 1989 and earned a master's degree in international affairs from George Washington University in 1992, where she joined Army ROTC. She served in the Illinois Army National Guard and was among the first handful of Army women to fly combat missions in the Iraq War.

After her injury she moved into public service focused on veterans. She directed the Illinois Department of Veterans' Affairs from 2006 to 2009, where her office helped create a veterans' employer tax credit and a first-in-the-nation 24-hour veterans crisis hotline. In 2009 President Obama appointed her an Assistant Secretary of Veterans Affairs, a post she held until 2011. She received the Purple Heart, and after 23 years in the Reserve Forces she retired from the military in 2014 as a lieutenant colonel.

Illinois voters elected her to the U.S. House, where she represented the 8th District for two terms (2013–2017), and then to the U.S. Senate in 2016, making her, in Britannica's words, the first U.S. senator born in Thailand. In 2018 she became the first sitting U.S. senator to give birth, and she won a rule change allowing senators to bring infants onto the Senate floor. As of October 2026 she serves as a U.S. senator from Illinois.
keyFacts: March 12, 1968: Born in Bangkok, Thailand.
November 12, 2004: Seriously wounded when her Black Hawk was hit in Iraq.
2009–2011: U.S. Assistant Secretary of Veterans Affairs.
2013–2017: U.S. Representative for Illinois's 8th District.
2017 to now, as of October 2026: U.S. Senator from Illinois.
2018: First U.S. senator to give birth while in office.
people.connectToWork: Duckworth's family once relied on public assistance, and later she helped design veterans' services after her own injury. Who with direct experience of your program helps shape it, and what power do they actually hold?

people.name: Charles Djou
body: When Charles Djou was sworn into the U.S. House in May 2010 after a surprise special-election win, he became only the second Republican since statehood to represent Hawaii in that chamber. He was born in Los Angeles on August 9, 1970. By the account of the U.S. House history office, his father was born in Shanghai and fled to Hong Kong during the Chinese Communist Revolution, and his mother grew up in Bangkok, Thailand. A 2012 U.S. Army article instead describes his mother as a refugee from the turmoil in Vietnam. The family moved to Hawaii when he was a boy, and he graduated from Punahou School in 1988.

Djou earned bachelor's degrees in political science and finance from the University of Pennsylvania in 1992 and a law degree from the University of Southern California in 1996. He served in the Hawaii House of Representatives from 2000 to 2002 as a Republican, and then on the Honolulu City Council from 2002 to 2010. He represented Hawaii's 1st Congressional District from May 22, 2010, to January 3, 2011.

Djou took a direct commission in the U.S. Army Reserve after the September 11, 2001 attacks. From 2011 to 2012, then a major serving as a judge advocate, he deployed to Kandahar Province, Afghanistan, with the 3rd Brigade Combat Team, 10th Mountain Division. The Association of the United States Army lists him as a colonel with a master's degree from the U.S. Army War College. He served as Secretary of the American Battle Monuments Commission, which cares for U.S. military cemeteries and memorials overseas. He held that post in August 2023 and when he testified to a House subcommittee in July 2024.
keyFacts: August 9, 1970: Born in Los Angeles.
2000–2002: Hawaii House of Representatives.
2002–2010: Honolulu City Council.
May 2010–January 2011: U.S. Representative, Hawaii 1st District.
2011–2012: Deployed to Kandahar, Afghanistan, with the U.S. Army Reserve.
July 2024: Testified to Congress as Secretary of the American Battle Monuments Commission.
people.connectToWork: Two official records describe Djou's mother's history differently. When your records and a person's own account of family or origin differ, how do you handle it, and who gets to say which is right?

people.name: Tiger Woods
body: When Tiger Woods was nine, his mother, Kultida "Tida" Woods, took him to Thailand for the first time. By the Associated Press's account, passing on her Thai heritage mattered to her. Woods later returned to Thailand to play three tournaments early in his professional career and won all three.

Kultida met Earl Woods in Bangkok, where she worked as a civilian secretary in a U.S. Army office. She moved to the United States in 1968, first to Brooklyn and then to Cypress, California, where Tiger was born on December 30, 1975. Britannica describes his father as African American and his mother as Thai.

Woods won 15 major championships. In April 2019, at age 43, he won his fifth Masters green jacket and 15th major, his first Masters title in 14 years, with his mother and his children watching. That same year he received the Presidential Medal of Freedom. When Kultida died in February 2025 at age 80, he called her a "force of nature."
keyFacts: 1968: Kultida Woods moved from Thailand to the U.S.
December 30, 1975: Tiger Woods born in Cypress, California.
2019: Won the Masters, his 15th major, and received the Presidential Medal of Freedom.
February 2025: Kultida Woods died at age 80.
people.connectToWork: Do your forms let someone record more than one heritage, and what happens to a Thai parent's language or family needs when a record shows only one box?

people.name: Pim Techamuanvivit
body: Pim Techamuanvivit's first job in a restaurant kitchen was at a restaurant she owned. She grew up in Bangkok, fed "really great food" by a nanny, and worked as a cognitive scientist doing design research in Silicon Valley before she gave up that career to cook. Her food blog, Chez Pim, launched in 2003 and was voted one of the most influential food blogs in the world by The Guardian.

In 2014 she opened Kin Khao in San Francisco, serving the Thai flavors she grew up with. It earned a Michelin star in 2015, a year in which she was treated for breast cancer and went to the award ceremony in a wheelchair. In late 2018 she took charge of the kitchen at Nahm, the Michelin-starred Thai restaurant in Bangkok's COMO Metropolitan Hotel, while keeping Kin Khao and splitting her time between the two cities. In 2019 she opened Nari, a second San Francisco restaurant, at Hotel Kabuki in Japantown; it earned a Michelin star in 2023.
keyFacts: Grew up in Bangkok; worked as a cognitive scientist in Silicon Valley.
2003: Launched the food blog Chez Pim.
2014: Opened Kin Khao in San Francisco.
2015: Kin Khao earned a Michelin star.
Late 2018: Became head chef of Nahm in Bangkok.
2019: Opened Nari in San Francisco (Michelin star 2023).
people.connectToWork: Techamuanvivit changed careers after a first profession in another field. When you assess someone's skills or goals, what would you ask to learn what they have done before, rather than judging from their current job?

people.name: Thakoon Panichgul
body: On the night Barack Obama accepted the Democratic presidential nomination in 2008, Michelle Obama wore a dress by Thakoon Panichgul. The moment put a Thai-born designer raised in Nebraska in front of a national audience.

Panichgul was born in Thailand and moved with his family to Omaha, Nebraska, at age 11. Sources name different provinces as his birthplace. He earned an undergraduate business degree from Boston University, worked as a buyer for J. Crew, and then took an editorial position at Harper's Bazaar. From 2001 to 2003 he took tailoring classes at Parsons School of Design in New York before launching his own label, Thakoon, with a 14-piece ready-to-wear collection in September 2004, sold exclusively through Net-a-Porter. In 2006 he was one of three winners of the Vogue/CFDA Fashion Fund, and the CFDA nominated him for its Swarovski Award for Best Emerging Womenswear Designer. He has collaborated with Gap, Mango and Target, and he later designed a collection for the department-store chain Kohl's.
keyFacts: Born in Thailand; moved to Omaha, Nebraska, at age 11.
Boston University business degree; Harper's Bazaar editor; Parsons tailoring classes 2001–2003.
September 2004: Launched his own label, Thakoon.
2006: Vogue/CFDA Fashion Fund winner.
2008: Michelle Obama wore his dress the night Obama accepted the Democratic nomination.
people.connectToWork: A child who moves to Minnesota at 11 may have been through a school system, and perhaps a language, before arriving. What does your process record about that move, and how would you use it?

people.name: Maurissa Tancharoen
body: Maurissa Tancharoen was diagnosed with lupus at 15. She went on to co-create and run a Marvel network drama, and she has long advocated for lupus awareness.

She grew up in Los Angeles' San Fernando Valley, where she started dancing almost as soon as she could walk, with the full support of her Thai immigrant parents. AsAm News has called her one of the few television executive producers who is Thai American. She has said that using her own last name in the credits "makes my mother and father proud."

Tancharoen started out as a teenage singer with a Motown band and went on to act, sing, dance, write and produce. Her brother, Kevin Tancharoen, directed the 2009 film Fame and Glee: The 3D Concert Movie. In 2008 she co-wrote the web musical Dr. Horrible's Sing-Along Blog, and she wrote for Fox's Dollhouse and Lifetime's Drop Dead Diva. With her husband, Jed Whedon, she co-created Marvel's Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D., which she ran as showrunner and executive producer through its seventh season.

Her lupus, which began with a butterfly rash, later caused lung, kidney and central nervous system flares, including one that left her for a time unable to walk, see or speak. She has rallied the cast and crew of her show for the Lupus Foundation of America's awareness campaigns, and in 2012 her friends and family, including her brother and brother-in-law Joss Whedon, formed a Los Angeles Walk to End Lupus Now team that raised nearly $80,000.
keyFacts: Raised in the San Fernando Valley by Thai immigrant parents.
Age 15: Diagnosed with lupus.
2008: Co-wrote Dr. Horrible's Sing-Along Blog.
Co-creator and showrunner of Marvel's Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D., which ran for seven seasons.
Longtime advocate for the Lupus Foundation of America.
people.connectToWork: Tancharoen's condition has changed over time, including periods when she could not walk, see or speak. Does your process plan for a condition that comes and goes, or does it assume someone's needs stay the same?

people.name: Jet Tila
body: Jet Tila grew up in a family that Food Network calls the "first family of Thai food." A Los Angeles native, he has continued his family's culinary legacy on and off screen, and Food Network describes his mastery of Thai and Chinese flavors.

Tila became a familiar face on Food Network as a chef, host, judge, and competitor on shows such as Ready Jet Cook, Tournament of Champions, Beat Bobby Flay, Guy's Grocery Games, Cutthroat Kitchen, Wildcard Kitchen and Halloween Cookie Challenge. He is a James Beard Award- and Emmy-nominated chef, restaurateur and author.

Tila grew up in Los Angeles' Thai Town and learned traditional cooking from his Cantonese grandmother. He describes himself as deeply rooted in his Thai Chinese culture, and he leads "Melting Pot Tours" of Thai Town. By the account of a chef profile from the Idaho Potato Commission, the Royal Thai Consul-General in Los Angeles appointed him the first Culinary Ambassador of Thai Cuisine.
keyFacts: Los Angeles native from the "first family of Thai food," in Food Network's words.
Food Network chef, host, judge and competitor; host of Ready Jet Cook.
James Beard Award- and Emmy-nominated chef, restaurateur and author.
First Culinary Ambassador of Thai Cuisine, named by the Royal Thai Consul-General in Los Angeles.
people.connectToWork: Tila describes himself as Thai Chinese, with a Cantonese grandmother. When you arrange language help or a cultural connection, how do you find out what a person actually speaks and identifies with, rather than going by a country on a form?

people.name: Cherry Chevapravatdumrong
body: "A lot of people watching the Family Guy credits think my name is fake," Cherry Chevapravatdumrong has said. "It's not. It's just Thai."

Originally from Ann Arbor, Michigan, she graduated from Huron High School, studied psychology at Yale and earned a law degree from New York University. She started writing TV spec scripts in law school, never took the bar exam, and moved to Los Angeles, where she took a job answering phones at an agency. She has been a writer and producer for Family Guy. As Cherry Cheva she has published two novels, She's So Money and DupliKate, and co-wrote It Takes a Village Idiot, and I Married One with Alex Borstein. Her short story "Talent Show" appeared in the 2013 anthology Open Mic: Riffs on Life Between Cultures in Ten Voices. In 2023 she co-wrote the Lionsgate comedy Joy Ride, directed by Adele Lim, with Teresa Hsiao, a friend she had worked with on Family Guy and Awkwafina Is Nora from Queens.
keyFacts: From Ann Arbor, Michigan; based in Los Angeles.
Psychology at Yale; law degree from NYU.
Writer and producer, Family Guy.
Novels as Cherry Cheva: She's So Money and DupliKate.
2023: Co-wrote Joy Ride with Teresa Hsiao.
people.connectToWork: Long names may be cut short, misspelled or doubted by a system or a person. How does your system handle a long name, and would you ask how the person wants it spelled and said?

people.name: Michelle Waterson-Gomez
body: Michelle Waterson-Gomez, known as "The Karate Hottie," turned professional in mixed martial arts in February 2007, when there was little money in the sport for women and no North American promotion devoted to them. She spent her first dozen fights on regional circuits such as Ring of Fire in Colorado and King of the Cage, going 9-3, before signing with the all-female promotion Invicta FC.

She grew up in Colorado with a mother who is half Thai and half Chinese and an American father. She earned a black belt in American freestyle karate and trained in wushu. Then she and her mother traveled to Thailand, where she spent about a month learning Muay Thai at the Sityodtong camp in Pattaya. She later said the trip "ignited my flame." She was raised Buddhist, and she has said her mother always told her to keep in mind the power of karma.

At Invicta she won the atomweight championship with a fourth-round submission of Jessica Penne and defended it once. She made her UFC debut in July 2015 with a third-round submission win, and over the next decade, based in Albuquerque, she faced three of the division's champions and headlined three cards. She retired after a unanimous-decision loss to Gillian Robertson at UFC 303 in Las Vegas on June 29, 2024, at age 38, with an overall record of 18-13.
keyFacts: February 2007: Professional mixed martial arts debut.
Won the Invicta FC atomweight title and defended it once.
July 2015: UFC debut, a submission win.
June 29, 2024: Retired after UFC 303 with an 18-13 record.
people.connectToWork: Waterson-Gomez has spoken about karma as a teaching from her mother that shaped her. If someone uses a religious word with you, how would you ask what it means to them, without deciding for them what it means?

people.name: Chanchanit Martorell
body: Before dawn on August 2, 1995, a multi-agency team raided a razor-wired apartment compound in El Monte, California. Inside, 72 Thai nationals had been forced to sew clothing, usually 16 hours a day, seven days a week, for about 69 cents an hour, under armed guard. Some had been held for as long as seven years. The Thai Community Development Center (Thai CDC), led by its founder and executive director Chanchanit Martorell, was part of the raid.

After the raid, immigration authorities held the workers for nine days while the Los Angeles Thai community worked to secure bonds and housing for their release. Thai CDC then gave them housing, food, clothing, medical care, legal help and English lessons. It led a Retailer Accountability Campaign aimed at the manufacturers and retailers that profited from the workers' labor and worked with legal aid groups on a civil suit, which won more than $4 million in restitution. In February 1996 the eight operators of the sweatshop pleaded guilty to conspiracy, involuntary servitude, and smuggling and harboring immigrants. By the Smithsonian's account, the case helped lead Congress to pass the Victims of Trafficking and Violence Protection Act of 2000, which created the T visa. The workers received visas with a path to citizenship.

Thai CDC was established in 1994. Martorell holds a Master of Urban Planning from UCLA and has taught a course on human trafficking and modern-day slavery there. California Humanities credits her with about six major human rights cases involving more than 400 Thai trafficking victims. By its account, Thai CDC played a key role in the eight-year organizing campaign that won Los Angeles's designation of Thai Town in 1999, and she founded the Thai New Year Songkran Festival there. As of October 2026 GuideStar lists her as executive director.
keyFacts: 1994: Thai Community Development Center established in Los Angeles.
August 2, 1995: Thai CDC took part in the El Monte raid that freed 72 Thai garment workers.
Workers later won more than $4 million in restitution.
October 27, 1999: Los Angeles designated Thai Town.
Holds a Master of Urban Planning from UCLA.
people.connectToWork: After the raid, a community organization helped frightened workers deal with agencies and courts. When someone has good reason to fear a government system, who could stand beside them in your process, and how would you find out whom they want?

people.name: Johnny Damon
body: In November 2012, after 18 seasons in the major leagues, Johnny Damon put on the uniform of Thailand's national baseball team. He was the only major leaguer on the roster as Thailand tried to qualify for the World Baseball Classic. In a text to a reporter he said he was "enjoying the experience of playing for my mom's country."

Damon was born on November 5, 1973, at Fort Riley, Kansas. His father, Jimmy, was a U.S. Army sergeant who met Johnny's mother, Yome, while serving in Thailand. Johnny's older brother, James, was born in Bangkok in 1971. The family moved from post to post before settling in Florida. Damon later remembered childhood visits to a Buddhist temple, monks sometimes visiting the family's home, and Thai food at the table. He credited his mother with teaching him to work hard.

The Kansas City Royals drafted Damon in the first round in 1992, and he turned down a baseball scholarship from the University of Florida to sign. He went on to play for the Royals, Athletics, Red Sox, Yankees, Tigers, Rays and Indians. He was an All-Star in 2002 and 2005. He won the World Series twice: with Boston in 2004, ending the team's 86-year championship drought, and with New York in 2009. He finished his career with 2,769 hits. In 2017 he was inducted into the Asian Hall of Fame in Seattle.
keyFacts: November 5, 1973: Born at Fort Riley, Kansas, to a Thai mother and a U.S. Army father.
1992: First-round draft pick of the Kansas City Royals.
2004 and 2009: World Series champion with Boston and New York.
2002 and 2005: American League All-Star.
2012: Played for Thailand in World Baseball Classic qualifying.
2017: Inducted into the Asian Hall of Fame.
people.connectToWork: Nothing in the name Johnny Damon tells you about a Thai mother or a childhood with temple visits. What in your process depends on guessing a person's background from a name, and what would you ask instead?

people.name: Rattawut Lapcharoensap
body: In 2005, Grove Press published Sightseeing, a book of short stories set in Thailand. The stories have titles like "Farangs," "Draft Day," "Priscilla the Cambodian" and "Cockfighter." The author, Rattawut Lapcharoensap, was in his mid-twenties.

Lapcharoensap was born in Chicago in 1979 and grew up in Bangkok, where he attended Triamudomsuksa Pattanakarn school. He returned to the United States for college at Cornell University, then earned a Master of Fine Arts in creative writing at the University of Michigan. There he won Michigan's Hopwood Award and the Andrea Beauchamp Prize, and he also received a David TK Wong Fellowship. His publisher announced that Sightseeing would appear in nine countries.

In 2006 the National Book Foundation named him one of its inaugural "5 Under 35" fiction writers, and Granta later named him one of its Best Young American Novelists. Sightseeing won the Asian American Literary Award and was a finalist for the Guardian First Book Award. In 2010 he received a Whiting Award, one of the major prizes for emerging American writers. He has since published stories in Granta, including "Valets" and "The Captain." Director Josh Kim adapted stories from Sightseeing, including "Draft Day," into the film How to Win at Checkers (Every Time). The Whiting Foundation says he teaches writing at Sarah Lawrence College.
keyFacts: 1979: Born in Chicago and raised in Bangkok.
Educated at Cornell University and the University of Michigan (MFA).
2005: Published the story collection Sightseeing (Grove Press).
2006: National Book Foundation "5 Under 35" honoree.
2010: Whiting Award.
people.connectToWork: Someone can be a U.S. citizen by birth and have spent childhood in another country. What does your process assume about schooling, language or familiarity with U.S. systems based on citizenship alone?

people.name: Pitchaya Sudbanthad
body: Pitchaya Sudbanthad's debut novel, Bangkok Wakes to Rain, was published by Riverhead Books on February 19, 2019. By the author's own account, both The New York Times and the Washington Post named it a notable book of the year, and it has been translated into French and Italian.

Sudbanthad grew up in Thailand, Saudi Arabia and the American South. Before the novel, he was a contributing writer at the online magazine The Morning News. He received a fiction fellowship from the New York Foundation for the Arts and a MacDowell fellowship in 2018, during which he revised his debut novel. MacDowell says he divides his time between Brooklyn and Bangkok.
keyFacts: Grew up in Thailand, Saudi Arabia and the American South.
Contributing writer at The Morning News.
New York Foundation for the Arts fiction fellowship. 2018: MacDowell fellowship.
2019: Published Bangkok Wakes to Rain.
people.connectToWork: Sudbanthad grew up in three places and lives between two cities. If your intake asks for one country of origin or one home address, what would you miss about someone's life, and what would you add?

people.name: Pimone Triplett
body: Pimone Triplett is a Thai American poet and a professor of creative writing in the University of Washington's MFA program in Seattle. She has published four collections of poetry: Ruining the Picture (Northwestern University Press, 1998), The Price of Light (Four Way Books, 2005), Rumor (Northwestern University Press, 2009) and Supply Chain (University of Iowa Press, 2017).

She holds an MFA from the University of Iowa and has taught in the MFA programs at Warren Wilson College and the University of Oregon and at the Kundiman Asian American Poetry Workshop. With Daniel Tobin, she co-edited Poet's Work, Poet's Play, a collection of essays on craft by professors in the Warren Wilson MFA Program. She has received publication awards and residencies from the Larry Levis Four Way Books Prize, the Oregon Book Award, the Bread Loaf Writers' Conference and the Fine Arts Work Center. The Academy of American Poets features her poems, including "Toy Peacock in Teak Birdcage" (2026).
keyFacts: Thai American poet; professor of creative writing, University of Washington MFA program.
Poetry collections published in 1998, 2005, 2009 and 2017.
MFA, University of Iowa; former faculty at Warren Wilson, University of Oregon and Kundiman.
Co-editor, with Daniel Tobin, of Poet's Work, Poet's Play.
Honors include the Larry Levis Four Way Books Prize and the Oregon Book Award.
people.connectToWork: When you picture who works in a field or who might advise your program, who comes to mind? Whose expertise, such as a Thai American professor's, might you be leaving out?

people.name: Nalutporn Krairiksh
body: Nalutporn Krairiksh is a Thai journalist based in Thailand. She is on this page for what she has said about disability, not as a Thai American. She was diagnosed with spinal muscular atrophy at age nine and uses a wheelchair. She graduated from Chulalongkorn University in 2015 and became a full-time reporter at Prachatai, a non-profit news site. In 2017 she founded ThisAble.Me, a sister site of Prachatai that focuses on disability issues.

Her work challenges coverage that treats disabled people as objects of pity or charity. In a 2021 profile by HaRDstories she said that prejudice tied to ideas about past deeds can lead people to accept their situation rather than work to change it, and she argued that a monthly allowance of 800 baht would not be so small if the government saw disabled people as full members of society. This is one advocate's view.
keyFacts: Diagnosed with spinal muscular atrophy at age nine; wheelchair user.
Graduated from Chulalongkorn University in 2015; then a reporter at Prachatai.
2017: Founded ThisAble.Me.
people.connectToWork: Krairiksh pushes back on some explanations of disability heard in Thailand. If a family member gives you one explanation, how would you also hear from the disabled person, who may see it differently?

institutions.name: Wat Thai of Minnesota
institutions.location: 2544 Highway 100 South, St. Louis Park, Minnesota
body: In February 2017, by the account of Asia Matters for America, hundreds of monks, Asian American families and curious neighbors filled a former Lutheran church in the Minneapolis suburbs for a New Year festival. The building had just been converted into a Buddhist temple. It was the newest home of Wat Thai of Minnesota, which had outgrown two earlier sites.

The temple began in late 2003, when a group of Minnesota Buddhists set out to create a place for worship and community. A donation from restaurateur Supenn Harrison made it possible, according to the same account. The temple itself dates its anniversaries from 2003 but says it was registered as a nonprofit, under the name Wat Pah Nanachat Minnesota, on April 22, 2004, at a Shorewood address, before it bought 28 acres in Becker. Asia Matters for America describes its first home as a house in Becker. In 2006 it moved to Elk River, but that site was about 45 minutes from Minneapolis and too small for regular events. The temple says it decided on January 9, 2017 to move to St. Louis Park. In early 2017 the temple's newly elected president, Dee Noree, bought the former Lutheran Church of the Reformation. The St. Louis Park Historical Society places that church at the temple's current address.

Today the temple, also known as Wat Promwachirayan, says on its About Us page that it has 10 resident monks (its GiveMN profile says at most 5) and offers public meditation on Wednesdays. Its GiveMN profile lists a weekly all-ages Thai dance class on Sundays, Thai cooking and language classes, free public events, and a library of English and Thai books on Buddhism and Thailand. In October 2024 it hosted a Royal Kathina ceremony with the Thai consulate in Chicago, and in September 2026 it hosted the MinnesoThai street food festival with the Thai Cultural Council of Minnesota.
keyFacts: Late 2003: Founded with a donation from Supenn Harrison. Registered as a nonprofit on April 22, 2004, as Wat Pah Nanachat Minnesota. First located in Becker.
2006: Moved to Elk River.
Early 2017: Moved into the former Lutheran Church of the Reformation.
Programs: meditation, Thai dance, language and cooking classes, and the Thai Cultural Group of MN.
institutions.connectToWork: Before you plan outreach through a temple, what do you know about who goes there and who does not? How would you ask the temple's leaders what they would want from your agency, if anything?

institutions.name: Thai Town, Los Angeles
body: On October 27, 1999, the Los Angeles City Council voted to name six blocks of Hollywood Boulevard, between Normandie and Western avenues, "Thai Town." The Los Angeles Times called it the nation's first. Councilwoman Jackie Goldberg backed the designation, and at a ceremony in January 2000 the city announced banners on the boulevard's lampposts and signs on the Hollywood Freeway marking it as a tourist destination.

California Humanities describes the vote as the result of an eight-year organizing campaign in which the Thai Community Development Center, led by its founder Chanchanit Martorell, played a key role. Today golden statues of apsonsi, mythical guardian figures, mark the neighborhood's entrances, and golden kinnara figures appear throughout Thai Town. By Thai CDC's account, in 2004 it secured $1.3 million from the city's Community Redevelopment Agency for Thai-style street lamps, banners, crosswalks, sidewalks and trees.

A 2000 Los Angeles Times report put Southern California's Thai population at about 80,000 and described East Hollywood as a point of entry for many of them, in a neighborhood shared with Latino, Armenian and other immigrant families. That figure is the newspaper's estimate from that year. In 2008 Thai Town and four other Asian Pacific Islander neighborhoods in Los Angeles received the federal Preserve America designation. Each April, Thai Town hosts the Songkran (Thai New Year) festival, with a parade.
keyFacts: October 27, 1999: Designated by the Los Angeles City Council.
Covers six blocks of Hollywood Boulevard between Normandie and Western avenues.
2004: $1.3 million streetscape grant secured by Thai CDC.
2008: Federal Preserve America designation.
Hosts an annual Songkran celebration in April.
institutions.connectToWork: Thai Town's recognition came through years of organizing, not large numbers. When your agency decides whom to involve or fund, how much weight goes to population size, and what could a smaller group's organizing tell you?

institutions.name: Thai Association of Minnesota
body: The Thai Association of Minnesota, also called ThaiAM, was established as a nonprofit in 1995, according to Asia Matters for America. ThaiAM's own events page lists a “Celebration of ThaiAM's 25th year Anniversary” on Oct. 13, 2019, which points to 1994, and its history page posts a 2013 article titled in Thai “Looking back 41 years of the Thai Association,” which points to an earlier association about 1972. The founding date is uncertain. Its goals include improving quality of life for people of Thai heritage, promoting Thai culture and language, and conveying Thai people's concerns and views to government agencies and the public. It predates the state's Thai temple, which was founded in 2003.

Its website describes it as a 501(c)(3) nonprofit that supports the well-being of the Thai community in Minnesota, and it reports on a Thai Picnic held in 2025. The Asia Matters article reports 3,200 Thai Americans in Minnesota, from a 2015 state demographic document. That is a single, older count that may not include everyone of Thai heritage, including people who report more than one background.
keyFacts: 1995: Established as a nonprofit, by Asia Matters for America's account; ThaiAM's own pages point to 1994 and about 1972.
Aims include quality of life for people of Thai heritage, Thai culture and language, and conveying views to government agencies and the public.
2025: Its website reports a Thai Picnic.
institutions.connectToWork: Before you contact an association like this one, what would you need to be clear about: what you are asking for, what you can pay for or change, and who else you are also hearing from?

institutions.name: PACER Center
institutions.type: Parent center for families of children with disabilities
body: PACER Center was established in 1977 by parents of children with disabilities, by its own account. It is a Minnesota organization that works to improve educational opportunities and quality of life for children and young adults with disabilities and their families. Its work covers parent training and advocacy, assistive technology, and social inclusion programs.

PACER is not a Thai organization. As of October 2026 its website links to Spanish and Somali sections and we saw no Thai materials. Its contact page says it has access to interpreters in multiple languages, on request.
keyFacts: Since 1977.
Focus areas: parent training and advocacy, assistive technology, social inclusion.
Interpreters available on request; phone 952-838-9000.
institutions.connectToWork: When you refer someone to a general resource, who checks that it works in their language? How would you find out whether the referral actually helped?

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. We did not find a study of how Thai Americans or Thai Minnesotans understand disability. The research below was done in Thailand, in small samples from Bangkok, and it says nothing certain about anyone living in Minnesota. Generation, time in the U.S., religion, region, class and education all differ, and some Thai Minnesotans have mixed family backgrounds.
questions: How do you and your family explain what's going on? What words do you use for it?
Who gave you a diagnosis or a label, and has it helped?
What do you want a label or assessment to open up for you? Is there anything you want it to avoid?
What do you hope for, for yourself or your family member?
Who helps with care, and who should be part of decisions? Is there anyone you do not want involved?
Are temple, prayer, merit-making or other faith practices a support for you? Are there dates we should plan around?
Would you like a Thai interpreter? Is there anyone you would not want as your interpreter, for privacy?
Who do you want to be able to see what you tell us?
Would it help to see examples of what training, work or living on your own can look like?
If you were caring for a parent, what would make outside help feel like support and not a replacement?

context.heading: One Bangkok study of caregivers and job training
body: Mallory (PLOS ONE, 2024) studied caregivers of neurodivergent adults in Bangkok: a focus group of 10 whose dependents had not started vocational training, and 13 whose dependents had recently finished it. Participants described karma and pressure to protect a family's image as things that could lead to denial or concealment. Some also described reframing, and some explained a child's autism openly. Caregivers reported limited information and services, and some avoided disability certification because of how it might affect work.

Caregivers whose dependents had finished training reported higher expectations, including one who said, "I realized she was capable of much more than I had thought." These were different people in the two groups, not the same people followed over time, so the study cannot show that training caused the change. The author notes a small sample from one provider, over-representing affluent families and expatriates, interviews in English, and an outside researcher who did not speak Thai. He calls it exploratory and not generalizable.

sources.label: Mallory, PLOS ONE (2024), "Capable of much more"

context.heading: One Bangkok study of mothers, faith and support
body: Tejakum, Truesdale and Cairns (2026) interviewed 12 Thai mothers of adolescents with intellectual disabilities, recruited through the Rajanukul Institute, a specialist service in Bangkok. Mothers described prayer, merit-making and temple attendance as sources of calm and strength, kept up selectively to fit caregiving, alongside formal services. They also described discrimination and unkind remarks, which discouraged them and often strengthened their resolve to advocate.

Mothers described themselves as main caregivers. Help from others ranged from essential to a source of conflict, including from stepparents and grandparents. Other parents and responsive professionals reduced isolation. The authors say the sample is small, from one specialist institute, and not generalizable.

sources.label: Tejakum, Truesdale and Cairns, Journal of Applied Research in Intellectual Disabilities (2026)

context.heading: Adult children caring for parents
body: A 1999 study of 15 adult children caring for frail parents in metropolitan Bangkok (Kespichayawattana) describes katanyu katavedi, meaning gratitude toward parents and the obligation to repay them, as helping to sustain family care. Effects on caregivers were positive, negative or mixed. It is an old, small study known to us from its abstract. Do not assume it applies to any family you work with. Ask.

sources.label: Kespichayawattana, Journal of Nursing Research, Innovation, and Health (1999), abstract

context.heading: Disagreement among Thai disabled advocates
body: Nalutporn Krairiksh, a disabled journalist in Thailand, argues against media coverage built on pity and charity, and against explanations that lead people to accept their situation rather than pursue access. Hers is one advocate's view, and it shows that no single explanation speaks for everyone in Thailand. Her profile is on this page.

sources.label: HaRDstories, "Nalutporn Krairiksh: Challenging Thai society to see people with disabilities as equally human" (2021)

context.heading: What this means when you prepare
body: Do not assume karma or any other explanation. Hear from the disabled person directly, even when a relative speaks first. Offer a trained Thai interpreter even when someone speaks some English, and check for privacy whether the interpreter knows the family. Explain who will see the information and how U.S. services work and who pays, because some people may not have used publicly funded services before. These are planning suggestions drawn from the studies above, not findings about Thai Minnesotans.

sources.label: Mallory, PLOS ONE (2024), "Capable of much more"
Tejakum, Truesdale and Cairns, Journal of Applied Research in Intellectual Disabilities (2026)

context.heading: What we could not find
body: We found no research on disability among Thai Americans, no source documenting Thai-language disability terms, nothing on traditional medicine for disability among Thai Americans, nothing on immigration-related fears or trust in U.S. systems in this group, and no Thai-specific disability organization in Minnesota or the U.S. Do not take this as a sign that such things are absent. Ask a qualified interpreter about terms, and ask each person which words they prefer.

organizations.intro: Minnesota's Thai organizations listed here center on Wat Thai of Minnesota in St. Louis Park, the Thai Association of Minnesota, the Thai Cultural Council of Minnesota and a University of Minnesota student association. The Thai consulate in Chicago and the embassy in Washington take part in events here. These are starting points for learning. The list is not complete, and listing here says nothing about who a person trusts. We did not check Facebook or LINE groups.

entries.name: Thai Cultural Council of Minnesota
entries.purpose: Organizes the Minnesota Songkran Festival (Thai New Year), held on the State Capitol grounds on May 10, 2025, and listed on a third-party 2026 events calendar at Wat Promwachirayan on May 16 and 17, 2026. That calendar is the only source for the 2026 dates and venue. It also runs the MinnesoThai street food festival, held September 19–20, 2026. The state's Legacy program lists a $25,000 grant for its May 2024 festival.

entries.purpose: By its GuideStar profile, advances the well-being of low- and moderate-income Thais and other communities in greater Los Angeles through human rights advocacy, affordable housing, health care access, small business promotion and neighborhood work.

entries.purpose: A professional association whose latest filing on record covers 2024. A related foundation, the Thai American Physician Foundation, held a conference in Atlanta in May 2026.

entries.purpose: Calls itself the leading association for Thai American business interests in California. It ran Dine Thai CA in June 2026.

entries.purpose: Thai-language news with sections on Thai life in the U.S. and on several U.S. cities. Its newest edition when we checked was dated October 30, 2026.
